verdict.rationale: Qdrant's docs describe in-database keyword-style matching through sparse vectors, which give 'precise word matching'. These can be fused with dense results via rrf/dbsf hybrid queries, so no separate search engine is needed. However, the evidence shows no native full-text index or text-match filter, and the sparse vectors must be supplied as embeddings rather than raw documents being searched directly. missing for 10: documented native full-text/BM25 indexing over raw text, tokenizer/analyzer configuration, independent hands-on corroboration of keyword search quality.

support.subject: As a developer, I can run keyword/full-text search over documents inside the database without bolting on a separate search engine

citations.quote: in text search, it is often useful to combine dense and sparse vectors to get the best of both worlds: semantic understanding from dense vectors and precise word matching from sparse vectors
Qdrant has a few ways of fusing the results from different queries: `rrf` and `dbsf`
Configure dense, sparse, and multi-vector embeddings.
